title: The Best Science-Based Full Body Workout for Size and Strength by Jeremy Ethier
summary: NH reviews Jeremy Ethier's two-day (A/B, 3x/week) science-based full body program. He attacks the 'science-based' marketing and its motto, then judges the program decent but ordinary: good selection on day A, too much deadlift volume and too much isolation on day B, and no C day for volume manipulation. He recommends the Bare Bones full body or his own novice program instead.
claims: 'Science-based' has become a gimmick and a meme that means nothing
You need to develop size and strength together, but to be really good you eventually have to specialise in one; chasing both makes you mediocre at both
Demanding scientific proof for every effort raises pampered lifters who never train while waiting for the perfect workout
Consistency trumps optimisation every time: a guy lifting rocks and doing chin-ups daily in a park beats someone doing a perfect workout once a week
If something gives you progress and results, keep doing it even if science or he disagrees; listen to your body
A scientific paper is still an opinion backed by facts; research can be skewed and most papers taken as gospel will be disproven within five years
Blind belief in science is as stupid as blind belief in opinions
Two-day A/B templates can get repetitive even for novices, though alternating means days don't fall on the same weekday
Full body three times a week is a great frequency for novices
Pages of EMG explanations of why the bench grows the chest are fluff to make a program look like hard work
Open with the back squat rather than bench because lower body lifts take more energy
Novices who can't do 6-10 pull-ups should just do what they can
Two exercises between presses is plenty of recovery; more spacing doesn't change pressing performance much
Face pulls belong at the end of a pushing session
Drag curls rely on sensation more than tension; novices should do standard curls and save drag curls as a later variation
Superset the OHP with pull-ups and finish with a giant set of leg curls, face pulls and curls to save time and boost conditioning
Novices lack the mental stamina to stay in the gym for long sessions
He can write a program like this in 25 minutes; the science packaging camouflages a plain mix of compounds and isolation
3-4 sets of 6-10 deadlifts is too much daily and weekly volume for novices; 1x5, 3x3 or 3x5 is enough
Evolving rep ranges for novices are good, but static schemes like 3x5 and 5x5 are popular because they are easy to progress
Don't give novices evolving rep ranges on the deadlift, especially at high volume
Full body programs with only two days lack options for volume manipulation; a C day is important
Too many isolation movements in a row means a day lacks substance; better manipulation of compounds is needed
Hyping science to novices is detrimental because it gets in their heads; a good program is good even written on a McDonald's bag
He stopped going to biology class at 14; programming for novices is not complicated
exercises: sensation over tension; use later as variation
better for novices than drag curls
